medical.title: How meal timing programs the liver's daily rhythms
medical.summary: Deep inside the brain, a master clock synchronizes thousands of molecular clocks scattered throughout the body, and together, they anticipate signals such as the rising sun, the coming night and the daily rhythms of life. But Texas A&M University researchers have discovered that the liver is also listening for another signal, one tuned to something much closer to home: the dinner bell.

medical.title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency may raise preterm birth risk, genetic analysis suggests
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Oulu have identified alpha-1 antitrypsin as a potential target for preventing spontaneous preterm birth. In a large genetic study of more than 200,000 mothers, a variant in the SERPINA1 gene, which encodes alpha-1 antitrypsin, was associated with shorter pregnancies.

medical.title: Stopping chronic pain before it starts: Surprising biological pathway may play key role
medical.summary: Chronic pain is one of medicine's most stubborn puzzles. A sprained back, a surgical incision or a pinched nerve heals—and yet, for millions of people, the pain never fully goes away. Why some injuries fade into memory while others evolve into a lifelong condition has remained largely a mystery.

medical.title: A decade without congenital syphilis: a Danish success story
medical.summary: Across Europe, cases of congenital syphilis nearly doubled in just one year, from 78 in 2023 to 140 in 2024, in 14 countries reporting data. In contrast, Denmark has marked 10 years without a single case of vertical syphilis transmission from mother to child since 2016.

medical.title: How severe illness during pregnancy sometimes alters neurodevelopment
medical.summary: Neurodevelopmental conditions, which include autism spectrum disorder, ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and more, affect around 10% of the American population. Despite their prevalence, it has remained difficult to pin down where, when and how many of these disorders begin.

medical.title: Five subtypes of common liver disease discovered—including rapidly progressing genetic forms
medical.summary: A liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide is not a single illness but five biologically distinct subtypes, Mayo Clinic researchers have found. Each carries different risks for heart disease, liver failure, cancer and the need for liver transplantation.

medical.title: Cannabis edibles can impair driving, even with blood THC below legal limits
medical.summary: The feeling of being "high" on cannabis primarily comes from its psychoactive compound, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC. Alongside it is its more subdued companion, cannabidiol (CBD), often used for its potential therapeutic benefits. THC is also found in many familiar edibles, from soft, chewy candies to brownies and chocolates, and can affect the brain when consumed.

medical.title: Assistance needed in Aisle 1: What Missouri WIC families face
medical.summary: The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children—better known as WIC—reaches an extraordinary share of American families. An estimated 41% of all U.S. infants participated in the federal nutrition program in fiscal year 2025, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

medical.title: Q&A: With peptide supplements, marketing outpaces the medicine
medical.summary: Peptides are short chunks of protein with specialized functions in the body. Insulin and GLP-1, both of which have U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval, are two of the most well-known.

medical.title: Diabetes drug metformin could be repurposed to help slow aging mechanisms
medical.summary: Metformin, a widely prescribed, safe and inexpensive drug for type 2 diabetes, is a first-line treatment that lowers blood sugar and improves the body's response to insulin. The drug appears to trick cells into sensing an energy shortage, similar to what happens during fasting or dieting. This activates a key cellular energy sensor called AMPK, which helps trigger cellular waste cleanup and supports cellular repair. Now, a recent review suggests metformin might also help counter some effects of aging.

medical.title: Experts say restricting junk food ads on public transport would pay off
medical.summary: Ever craved fast food after seeing an enticing ad on a bus or at a train station? Such powerful advertisements increase consumption of unhealthy foods and drinks, contributing to obesity, which costs Australia's health care system and society an estimated A$39 billion each year.

medical.title: Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill.

medical.title: Are petting zoos safe?
medical.summary: A 3-year-old girl has died from a rare illness after visiting a petting zoo in Victoria. She developed brain damage and kidney failure after spending weeks in intensive care.

medical.title: New disease gene discovery provides answers to families
medical.summary: Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka researchers have helped identify the cause of a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disorder. Dr. Meghan Mulligan, of the Department of Biochemistry, says the finding has given people around the world an answer to the source of their family member's neurological condition.

medical.title: More frequent cannabis use linked to poorer mental health
medical.summary: More frequent cannabis use is associated with fewer days of good mental health among adults, particularly men, according to a study co-authored by a University of Miami Business School professor.

medical.title: Study uncovers why some immunotherapy-treated tumors may grow faster
medical.summary: A new Northwestern Medicine study has uncovered a biological mechanism that may explain why a subset of tumors unexpectedly grows at an accelerated rate after being treated with certain immunotherapies, according to findings published in the journal Cancer Discovery.

medical.title: Immune drug anifrolumab linked to lower risk of infection and hospitalization for skin lupus
medical.summary: Preliminary results from an investigator-initiated, single-site clinical study show that some people with chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus—a type of lupus that can cause permanent skin damage and hair loss—are less likely to acquire life-threatening infections when taking the drug anifrolumab, an FDA-approved monoclonal antibody treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus.

medical.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
medical.summary: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful.

medical.title: Keto diet cut liver fat by 67% in a clinical trial
medical.summary: A ketogenic diet outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in several measures of metabolic health during a clinical trial involving people with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. All three groups lost about 10% of their body weight, but keto reduced liver fat by 67%, compared with 45% for the other diets. About half of the keto group also no longer qualified as having prediabetes after four to five months.

medical.title: Dogs may hold surprising clues to human longevity
medical.summary: Dogs and humans may have more in common when it comes to aging than scientists realized. Researchers with the Dog Aging Project found that patterns of small molecules in dogs’ blood were linked to longer or shorter lifespans in remarkably similar ways to those seen in people. These metabolic “fingerprints” could offer clues about the biological processes that drive aging, including metabolism, inflammation, and cellular stress.

medical.title: Long-term melatonin use linked to 90% higher heart failure risk
medical.summary: People with chronic insomnia who used melatonin long term had a roughly 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years, according to a large preliminary study. The findings do not prove melatonin causes heart problems, but they raise new questions about the safety of taking the popular sleep supplement for extended periods.

medical.title: What went right this week: an ‘historic’ fall in violent crime, plus more
medical.summary: A ‘historic’ fall in US violent crime, Europe’s right to repair law, and a conservation triumph for Kazakhstan, plus more The post What went right this week: an ‘historic’ fall in violent crime, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Common medications may change your gut for years
medical.summary: Common medications may reshape the gut microbiome long after the last dose is taken. In a study of more than 2,500 people, researchers found lasting microbial changes linked not only to antibiotics, but also to antidepressants, beta-blockers, acid-reducing drugs, and benzodiazepines. Some effects were still detectable years later, suggesting past medication use may strongly influence the gut bacteria people carry today.

medical.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
medical.summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

medical.title: Gut bacteria may unlock a hidden benefit of vegetables
medical.summary: Gut bacteria can transform nitrate and plant-based iron from vegetables and other foods into protective molecules that may benefit the heart and metabolism. In experimental models, higher levels of these compounds were linked to lower blood pressure, better blood sugar control, healthier blood vessels, and less liver fat.

science.title: Tiny crustacean helps scientists understand genes regulating circatidal rhythms
science.summary: Scientists at UMass Chan Medical School and the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole have shown that the four core clock genes responsible for maintaining circadian rhythms in animals—Per, Cry2, Bmal1 and Clk—also regulate circatidal behavior in the crustacean P. hawaiensis.

science.title: Igniting Roman’s Journey
science.summary: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT on Aug. 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Roman pairs a large […]

science.title: Can Australian businesses legally ban customers from using smart glasses?
science.summary: Businesses and local councils around Australia are increasingly imposing their own restrictions on "smart glasses," responding to customers' concerns about being covertly recorded in public places.

science.title: Dual-purpose qubit design could speed operations while cutting quantum errors
science.summary: Researchers from MIT have designed a new qubit architecture that enables qubits to interact with each other much more quickly while remaining very stable. This advance could someday help scientists build practical quantum computers that can run long, complex algorithms with high accuracy.

science.title: First DDT, now the flu: Peregrine falcons in San Francisco Bay Area hit hard by H5N1 variant
science.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) featured prominently in the news during 2020 as it took the lives of millions of birds across the globe. While the worst seems to be behind us, population-level effects are just now emerging.

science.title: Who hears you say 'thank you?' It matters more than you might think
science.summary: There are many ways to say thank you.

science.title: Quantum control algorithm looks to explain how birds migrate
science.summary: The hidden world of quantum mechanics exists at scales many orders of magnitude smaller than living organisms, yet scientists have long theorized that quantum effects play an important role in biology. Birds' ability to sense magnetic fields during migration is one of the best-known mysteries in this field, with leading theories suggesting that this sensing could be achieved by exploiting quantum entanglement.

science.title: Why feeding birds can make you feel better
science.summary: More than 56 million U.S. adults feed wild birds.

science.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Superbubble Scene
science.summary: This Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista called N44.

science.title: Ancient “living fossils” may reveal how complex life began
science.summary: A newly discovered microbe living inside ancient stromatolite communities may offer a rare look at how complex life first emerged. Researchers captured the first direct images of an Asgard archaeon physically connected to a bacterium, with the two microbes appearing to exchange nutrients and other compounds. Scientists think similar partnerships billions of years ago may have helped produce the first complex cells.

science.title: Overqualification can make or break family life, study reveals
science.summary: New research shows overqualified employees who prioritize work over family are more likely to let anxiety and fear about their careers spill into their home lives, creating damaging conflict.

science.title: NASA scientists discover a giant 10-sided pattern on Saturn
science.summary: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades.

science.title: Can an AI tutor help students improve at math?
science.summary: As schools contend with rapid developments in artificial intelligence, new research from the University of Toronto Mississauga suggests an AI tutor could help students with math, but only if it holds back answers and coaches them through problems.

science.title: Our pay is called a 'salary,' but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?
science.summary: Every other Wednesday, like clockwork, my salary arrives in my bank account. By Thursday, most of it is gone.

science.title: Scientists just overturned a century-old physics assumption
science.summary: Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University have discovered an unexpected form of the Hall effect, overturning the long-held assumption that this electrical response only appears when a magnetic field points perpendicular to a material. Beyond expanding a century-old principle of physics, the finding could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors for electronics, transportation, and medical technologies.

science.title: Looking back to forecast the future of lobster
science.summary: For generations, the lobster fishery has been central to the cultural and economic identity of Maine and Atlantic Canada. Predicting what the future holds for the species—and the people who depend on it—has long been a priority for scientists and resource managers.

science.title: Salt may have helped turn Earth into a frozen world 700 million years ago
science.summary: Earth may have been pushed deeper into a global deep freeze by something surprisingly ordinary: salt. Around 700 million years ago, Earth entered periods of extreme glaciation known as Snowball Earth, when ice is thought to have spread across much or potentially all of the planet's surface. Scientists have long known that expanding ice could have helped drive this transition: As bright ice replaces darker ocean water, more sunlight is reflected back into space, causing the planet to cool further and allowing even more ice to form.

science.title: Informal supporters share experiences of NDIS behavior support practitioners
science.summary: A new national survey of informal supporters of people with disabilities who have received NDIS-funded behavior support services has identified wide variation in supporters' confidence in practitioners' knowledge and skills, pointing to a need for greater transparency about practitioner expertise and stronger, more consistent, rights-based behavior support across the NDIS.

science.title: Why Britons disagree about poverty: They draw the line differently
science.summary: People with different political beliefs do not only disagree about how much poverty exists in Britain but they also differ over whether the same material circumstances should be defined as poverty, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management.

science.title: Scientists turn one of the hardest plastics to recycle into high-performance engine lubricant
science.summary: Researchers have discovered a way to turn notoriously difficult-to-recycle PVC plastic into a key ingredient used in high-performance lubricants such as engine oil. The technique could give mountains of plastic waste a valuable second life while making lubricant production more sustainable.

science.title: The universe is still speeding up, but nobody knows why
science.summary: A major new analysis challenges recent claims that the universe's expansion is slowing, finding that the evidence for cosmic acceleration remains strong. The findings preserve the leading role of dark energy, while leaving scientists with the enduring mystery of what this strange cosmic force actually is.

science.title: Australia’s red soil may be hiding a massive clean energy source
science.summary: Researchers have discovered that Western Australia’s iron-rich rocks can naturally generate hydrogen and that the process may be boosted to produce much larger amounts. If it can be scaled up, the vast formations beneath the Pilbara could become a major new source of low-emission energy for Australia and potentially the world.

environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: How meal timing programs the liver's daily rhythms
mix_items.summary: Deep inside the brain, a master clock synchronizes thousands of molecular clocks scattered throughout the body, and together, they anticipate signals such as the rising sun, the coming night and the daily rhythms of life. But Texas A&M University researchers have discovered that the liver is also listening for another signal, one tuned to something much closer to home: the dinner bell.

mix_items.title: Tiny crustacean helps scientists understand genes regulating circatidal rhythms
mix_items.summary: Scientists at UMass Chan Medical School and the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole have shown that the four core clock genes responsible for maintaining circadian rhythms in animals—Per, Cry2, Bmal1 and Clk—also regulate circatidal behavior in the crustacean P. hawaiensis.

mix_items.summary: Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. mix_items.title: Can Australian businesses legally ban customers from using smart glasses?
mix_items.summary: Businesses and local councils around Australia are increasingly imposing their own restrictions on "smart glasses," responding to customers' concerns about being covertly recorded in public places.

mix_items.title: Dual-purpose qubit design could speed operations while cutting quantum errors
mix_items.summary: Researchers from MIT have designed a new qubit architecture that enables qubits to interact with each other much more quickly while remaining very stable. This advance could someday help scientists build practical quantum computers that can run long, complex algorithms with high accuracy.

mix_items.title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency may raise preterm birth risk, genetic analysis suggests
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Oulu have identified alpha-1 antitrypsin as a potential target for preventing spontaneous preterm birth. In a large genetic study of more than 200,000 mothers, a variant in the SERPINA1 gene, which encodes alpha-1 antitrypsin, was associated with shorter pregnancies.

mix_items.title: Stopping chronic pain before it starts: Surprising biological pathway may play key role
mix_items.summary: Chronic pain is one of medicine's most stubborn puzzles. A sprained back, a surgical incision or a pinched nerve heals—and yet, for millions of people, the pain never fully goes away. Why some injuries fade into memory while others evolve into a lifelong condition has remained largely a mystery.

mix_items.title: A decade without congenital syphilis: a Danish success story
mix_items.summary: Across Europe, cases of congenital syphilis nearly doubled in just one year, from 78 in 2023 to 140 in 2024, in 14 countries reporting data. In contrast, Denmark has marked 10 years without a single case of vertical syphilis transmission from mother to child since 2016.

mix_items.title: How severe illness during pregnancy sometimes alters neurodevelopment
mix_items.summary: Neurodevelopmental conditions, which include autism spectrum disorder, ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and more, affect around 10% of the American population. Despite their prevalence, it has remained difficult to pin down where, when and how many of these disorders begin.

mix_items.title: First DDT, now the flu: Peregrine falcons in San Francisco Bay Area hit hard by H5N1 variant
mix_items.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) featured prominently in the news during 2020 as it took the lives of millions of birds across the globe. While the worst seems to be behind us, population-level effects are just now emerging.

mix_items.title: Who hears you say 'thank you?' It matters more than you might think
mix_items.summary: There are many ways to say thank you.

mix_items.title: Five subtypes of common liver disease discovered—including rapidly progressing genetic forms
mix_items.summary: A liver disease affecting nearly 30% of adults worldwide is not a single illness but five biologically distinct subtypes, Mayo Clinic researchers have found. Each carries different risks for heart disease, liver failure, cancer and the need for liver transplantation.

mix_items.title: Quantum control algorithm looks to explain how birds migrate
mix_items.summary: The hidden world of quantum mechanics exists at scales many orders of magnitude smaller than living organisms, yet scientists have long theorized that quantum effects play an important role in biology. Birds' ability to sense magnetic fields during migration is one of the best-known mysteries in this field, with leading theories suggesting that this sensing could be achieved by exploiting quantum entanglement.

mix_items.title: Why feeding birds can make you feel better
mix_items.summary: More than 56 million U.S. adults feed wild birds.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Hubble Spies Superbubble Scene
mix_items.summary: This Hubble Space Telescope image features a sprawling cosmic vista called N44.

mix_items.title: Ancient “living fossils” may reveal how complex life began
mix_items.summary: A newly discovered microbe living inside ancient stromatolite communities may offer a rare look at how complex life first emerged. Researchers captured the first direct images of an Asgard archaeon physically connected to a bacterium, with the two microbes appearing to exchange nutrients and other compounds. Scientists think similar partnerships billions of years ago may have helped produce the first complex cells.

mix_items.title: Cannabis edibles can impair driving, even with blood THC below legal limits
mix_items.summary: The feeling of being "high" on cannabis primarily comes from its psychoactive compound, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC. Alongside it is its more subdued companion, cannabidiol (CBD), often used for its potential therapeutic benefits. THC is also found in many familiar edibles, from soft, chewy candies to brownies and chocolates, and can affect the brain when consumed.

mix_items.title: Overqualification can make or break family life, study reveals
mix_items.summary: New research shows overqualified employees who prioritize work over family are more likely to let anxiety and fear about their careers spill into their home lives, creating damaging conflict.

mix_items.title: NASA scientists discover a giant 10-sided pattern on Saturn
mix_items.summary: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades.

mix_items.title: Assistance needed in Aisle 1: What Missouri WIC families face
mix_items.summary: The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children—better known as WIC—reaches an extraordinary share of American families. An estimated 41% of all U.S. infants participated in the federal nutrition program in fiscal year 2025, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

mix_items.title: Can an AI tutor help students improve at math?
mix_items.summary: As schools contend with rapid developments in artificial intelligence, new research from the University of Toronto Mississauga suggests an AI tutor could help students with math, but only if it holds back answers and coaches them through problems.

mix_items.title: Q&A: With peptide supplements, marketing outpaces the medicine
mix_items.summary: Peptides are short chunks of protein with specialized functions in the body. Insulin and GLP-1, both of which have U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval, are two of the most well-known.

mix_items.title: Our pay is called a 'salary,' but were Roman soldiers really paid in salt?
mix_items.summary: Every other Wednesday, like clockwork, my salary arrives in my bank account. By Thursday, most of it is gone.

mix_items.title: Diabetes drug metformin could be repurposed to help slow aging mechanisms
mix_items.summary: Metformin, a widely prescribed, safe and inexpensive drug for type 2 diabetes, is a first-line treatment that lowers blood sugar and improves the body's response to insulin. The drug appears to trick cells into sensing an energy shortage, similar to what happens during fasting or dieting. This activates a key cellular energy sensor called AMPK, which helps trigger cellular waste cleanup and supports cellular repair. Now, a recent review suggests metformin might also help counter some effects of aging.

mix_items.title: Scientists just overturned a century-old physics assumption
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University have discovered an unexpected form of the Hall effect, overturning the long-held assumption that this electrical response only appears when a magnetic field points perpendicular to a material. Beyond expanding a century-old principle of physics, the finding could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors for electronics, transportation, and medical technologies.

mix_items.title: Looking back to forecast the future of lobster
mix_items.summary: For generations, the lobster fishery has been central to the cultural and economic identity of Maine and Atlantic Canada. Predicting what the future holds for the species—and the people who depend on it—has long been a priority for scientists and resource managers.

mix_items.title: Experts say restricting junk food ads on public transport would pay off
mix_items.summary: Ever craved fast food after seeing an enticing ad on a bus or at a train station? Such powerful advertisements increase consumption of unhealthy foods and drinks, contributing to obesity, which costs Australia's health care system and society an estimated A$39 billion each year.

mix_items.title: Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill.

mix_items.title: Salt may have helped turn Earth into a frozen world 700 million years ago
mix_items.summary: Earth may have been pushed deeper into a global deep freeze by something surprisingly ordinary: salt. Around 700 million years ago, Earth entered periods of extreme glaciation known as Snowball Earth, when ice is thought to have spread across much or potentially all of the planet's surface. Scientists have long known that expanding ice could have helped drive this transition: As bright ice replaces darker ocean water, more sunlight is reflected back into space, causing the planet to cool further and allowing even more ice to form.

mix_items.title: Are petting zoos safe?
mix_items.summary: A 3-year-old girl has died from a rare illness after visiting a petting zoo in Victoria. She developed brain damage and kidney failure after spending weeks in intensive care.

mix_items.title: New disease gene discovery provides answers to families
mix_items.summary: Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka researchers have helped identify the cause of a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disorder. Dr. Meghan Mulligan, of the Department of Biochemistry, says the finding has given people around the world an answer to the source of their family member's neurological condition.

mix_items.title: More frequent cannabis use linked to poorer mental health
mix_items.summary: More frequent cannabis use is associated with fewer days of good mental health among adults, particularly men, according to a study co-authored by a University of Miami Business School professor.

mix_items.title: Study uncovers why some immunotherapy-treated tumors may grow faster
mix_items.summary: A new Northwestern Medicine study has uncovered a biological mechanism that may explain why a subset of tumors unexpectedly grows at an accelerated rate after being treated with certain immunotherapies, according to findings published in the journal Cancer Discovery.

mix_items.title: Informal supporters share experiences of NDIS behavior support practitioners
mix_items.summary: A new national survey of informal supporters of people with disabilities who have received NDIS-funded behavior support services has identified wide variation in supporters' confidence in practitioners' knowledge and skills, pointing to a need for greater transparency about practitioner expertise and stronger, more consistent, rights-based behavior support across the NDIS.

mix_items.title: Why Britons disagree about poverty: They draw the line differently
mix_items.summary: People with different political beliefs do not only disagree about how much poverty exists in Britain but they also differ over whether the same material circumstances should be defined as poverty, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management.

mix_items.title: Immune drug anifrolumab linked to lower risk of infection and hospitalization for skin lupus
mix_items.summary: Preliminary results from an investigator-initiated, single-site clinical study show that some people with chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus—a type of lupus that can cause permanent skin damage and hair loss—are less likely to acquire life-threatening infections when taking the drug anifrolumab, an FDA-approved monoclonal antibody treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus.

mix_items.title: One immune switch may help drive aging across the body
mix_items.summary: Aging may be partly fueled by immune cells losing their ability to clear away damaged, inflammation-promoting cells. Blocking a single receptor restored that cleanup process in mice, reducing inflammation and helping their organs, muscles, and memory remain remarkably youthful.

mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: Keto diet cut liver fat by 67% in a clinical trial
mix_items.summary: A ketogenic diet outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in several measures of metabolic health during a clinical trial involving people with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. All three groups lost about 10% of their body weight, but keto reduced liver fat by 67%, compared with 45% for the other diets. About half of the keto group also no longer qualified as having prediabetes after four to five months.

mix_items.title: Dogs may hold surprising clues to human longevity
mix_items.summary: Dogs and humans may have more in common when it comes to aging than scientists realized. Researchers with the Dog Aging Project found that patterns of small molecules in dogs’ blood were linked to longer or shorter lifespans in remarkably similar ways to those seen in people. These metabolic “fingerprints” could offer clues about the biological processes that drive aging, including metabolism, inflammation, and cellular stress.

mix_items.title: Scientists turn one of the hardest plastics to recycle into high-performance engine lubricant
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered a way to turn notoriously difficult-to-recycle PVC plastic into a key ingredient used in high-performance lubricants such as engine oil. The technique could give mountains of plastic waste a valuable second life while making lubricant production more sustainable.

mix_items.title: The universe is still speeding up, but nobody knows why
mix_items.summary: A major new analysis challenges recent claims that the universe's expansion is slowing, finding that the evidence for cosmic acceleration remains strong. The findings preserve the leading role of dark energy, while leaving scientists with the enduring mystery of what this strange cosmic force actually is.

mix_items.title: Long-term melatonin use linked to 90% higher heart failure risk
mix_items.summary: People with chronic insomnia who used melatonin long term had a roughly 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years, according to a large preliminary study. The findings do not prove melatonin causes heart problems, but they raise new questions about the safety of taking the popular sleep supplement for extended periods.

mix_items.title: Australia’s red soil may be hiding a massive clean energy source
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered that Western Australia’s iron-rich rocks can naturally generate hydrogen and that the process may be boosted to produce much larger amounts. If it can be scaled up, the vast formations beneath the Pilbara could become a major new source of low-emission energy for Australia and potentially the world.

mix_items.title: What went right this week: an ‘historic’ fall in violent crime, plus more
mix_items.summary: A ‘historic’ fall in US violent crime, Europe’s right to repair law, and a conservation triumph for Kazakhstan, plus more The post What went right this week: an ‘historic’ fall in violent crime, plus more appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: Common medications may change your gut for years
mix_items.summary: Common medications may reshape the gut microbiome long after the last dose is taken. In a study of more than 2,500 people, researchers found lasting microbial changes linked not only to antibiotics, but also to antidepressants, beta-blockers, acid-reducing drugs, and benzodiazepines. Some effects were still detectable years later, suggesting past medication use may strongly influence the gut bacteria people carry today.

mix_items.title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
mix_items.summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

mix_items.title: Gut bacteria may unlock a hidden benefit of vegetables
mix_items.summary: Gut bacteria can transform nitrate and plant-based iron from vegetables and other foods into protective molecules that may benefit the heart and metabolism. In experimental models, higher levels of these compounds were linked to lower blood pressure, better blood sugar control, healthier blood vessels, and less liver fat.

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
